results.name: AI Agent Orchestration & Meta-Harnesses
results.result:
Tech journalists, developer publications, and practitioners report **LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Google ADK** as the primary production-ready agent orchestration frameworks in 2026, with **LangGraph** positioned as the default for stateful, regulated workflows[1][2].

### Framework-Specific Analysis (OpenAI Agents SDK, Semantic Kernel, Haystack, Mastra, smolagents, Google ADK, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, Omnigent)

| Framework | Published Benchmarks / Adoption Reports | Native Claude Support | Problem Class Solved Better Than LangGraph |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** (Handoff-based) | Stabilized as a main production leader; offers durable execution, checkpointing, and first-class human-in-the-loop primitives[1]. | **No** (Native support is for OpenAI models; Claude requires external integration) | **Simple handoff logic** for linear workflows where isolating decision points is less critical than rapid handoff between agents[1]. |
| **Semantic Kernel** (Now part of Microsoft Agent Framework) | Merged into Microsoft Agent Framework (reached v1.0 GA in April 2026); the unified successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel[1][2]. | **No** (Requires external integration via Microsoft Agent Framework) | **Legacy .NET/Azure integration**; provides a unified graph-based workflow for teams already inside the Microsoft ecosystem where semantic plugin orchestration is paramount[2]. |
| **Haystack** (RAG-focused) | Purpose-built for RAG and document processing; used for customizable LLM applications and RAG pipelines[3]. | **No** (Requires external integration) | **RAG and document-heavy pipelines**; solves custom LLM application building and data ingestion better than LangGraph’s general stateful graph focus[3]. |
| **Mastra** | Not listed among the five main production leaders in 2026 verified data; likely a developer framework or emerging tool[1]. | Unknown (Likely **No** natively) | Not clearly defined as solving a class *better* than LangGraph in 2026 production reports. |
| **smolagents** (Single-agent loops) | Minimizes overhead for single-agent loops; listed among top open-source solutions but not a main production leader[1][3]. | **No** (Requires external integration) | **Single-agent loops with minimal overhead**; optimized for lightweight, low-latency single-agent tasks where LangGraph’s graph complexity is unnecessary[3]. |
| **Google ADK** (Hierarchical) | One of the five main production leaders; uses a hierarchical pattern that "actually ships" for complex, multi-layered orchestration[1][4]. | **No** (Native support is for Gemini; Claude requires external integration) | **Hierarchical multi-layer orchestration**; solves complex, multi-tier agent systems where high-level planning and sub-agent delegation are more critical than fine-grained state transitions[1]. |
| **CrewAI** (Role-based) | 5K+ GitHub stars, 1,500+ company adoptions; fastest path from idea to prototype but teams often outgrow its role-based simplicity in production[1][2][5]. | **No** (Requires external integration, e.g., via LangChain) | **Rapid prototyping with intuitive role-based mental models**; faster for initial multi-agent team setup than LangGraph, though less robust for complex state management[1][2]. |
| **Microsoft Agent Framework** (Graph-based) | Unified successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel (v1.0 GA April 2026); default for .NET/Azure-native teams with graph-based workflows and Azure AI guardrails[1][2]. | **No** (Requires external integration via Azure AI or custom connectors) | **Enterprise .NET/Azure integration with graph-based workflows**; provides graph-based orchestration with responsible AI guardrails specifically for Microsoft stacks, whereas LangGraph is Python-centric[2]. |
| **Omnigent** | Not listed among the 15 frameworks with verified production data in 2026; likely not a production leader[1]. | Unknown | Not defined in 2026 production reports as solving a class better than LangGraph. |

### What Practenders Chose When Moving Off LangChain/LangGraph

Practitioners moving off **LangChain** (for prototyping) or **LangGraph** (for advanced stateful workflows) typically choose **CrewAI** for rapid role-based prototyping or **Microsoft Agent Framework** / **OpenAI Agents SDK** for specific enterprise stack integrations (Azure/.NET or handoff-heavy workflows)[1][2].

*   **From LangChain:** Teams choose **CrewAI** for its intuitive role-based model to build prototypes quickly, migrating to LangGraph only when production complexity hits the "ceiling" of role-based orchestration[1][2].
*   **From LangGraph:** Teams rarely move *off* LangGraph for production agent work unless they need **specific ecosystem integration** (e.g., **Microsoft Agent Framework** for .NET/Azure) or **simpler handoff logic** (e.g., **OpenAI Agents SDK**) where the cost of LangGraph’s fine-grained state control is unnecessary[1][2].
*   **Key Shift:** The consensus is that **LangGraph** remains the "consensus choice for serious production agentic AI deployments in 2026" due to its durable execution, checkpointing, and auditability[1]. Teams moving *off* it often do so because their workflows are **linear** (favoring **CrewAI**) or **hierarchical** (favoring **Google ADK**) rather than requiring complex, stateful graph branching[1].

**Summary:** Tech media states that when practitioners move off LangChain/LangGraph, they choose **CrewAI** for speed-to-prototype or **Microsoft Agent Framework/OpenAI Agents SDK** for ecosystem-specific needs, but **LangGraph** is still the default for stateful, regulated production workflows[1][2].

results.name: AI Security & PII Governance
results.result:
In 2026, the most effective tools for preventing client PII from reaching untrusted LLMs are **local Python libraries** (like Microsoft Presidio and Scrubadub, plus the newer **effGen** and **effGen**-derived guardrails) combined with **open-source API gateways** (such as **Portkey**) that offer inline PII redaction and prompt injection detection.

### 1. Local PII Redaction Libraries (Code-Level)
These libraries run directly in your Python application, scrubbing names, booking references, and payment data before the query is sent to an open-source model.

*   **Microsoft Presidio**: The industry-standard open-source library for PII detection and redaction. It supports custom models and regex patterns to catch booking references and payment data.
    *   *Key Feature*: Reversible anonymization (encryption) and tokenization (e.g., `[NAME_1]`).
*   **Scrubadub (ABN)**: A lightweight Python library specifically designed for removing PII from text with minimal dependencies.
    *   *Key Feature*: Fast, regex-based removal of emails, phone numbers, and names.
*   **effGen (ICML 2026)**: A newer, high-performance library with built-in `Redactor` and `Guardrail` presets.
    *   *Key Feature*: Automatically strips OpenAI, Anthropic, and other provider webhook patterns (API keys, secrets) at the encoder level, ensuring no secrets appear in logs [2].
    *   *Guardrails*: Includes one-liner access to strict PII detection and prompt injection blocking via `get_guardrail_preset("strict")` [2].
*   **Gladia’s PII Redaction**: While often an API, it offers **native Python and TypeScript libraries** for local ecosystem integration.
    *   *Key Feature*: Supports 40+ entity types (including GDPR, HIPAA, PCI) and allows flexible output modes like `MASK` or `MARKER` (e.g., `[NAME_1]`) [5].

### 2. API Gateway PII Filters & Prompt Injection Detectors
Open-source gateways act as a middleware layer between your code and the LLM, enforcing security policies without requiring enterprise SaaS.

*   **Portkey**: An open-source AI gateway available as a self-hosted solution that bundles observability with **inline guardrails**.
    *   *Key Feature*: Runs **PII redaction** and **prompt injection detection** on *each request* before forwarding to the LLM [10].
    *   *Proxy*: Acts as a proxy that intercepts and sanitizes data transparently.
*   **effGen Guardrails**: As noted above, the `effGen` library provides a "strict" guardrail preset that includes **prompt injection blocking** and **toxicity filtering** directly in the Python code [2].

### 3. Audit Trail Tools for AI Outputs
To track what data was redacted and ensure compliance, you need Python-native logging and tracing solutions.

*   **effGen Structured Logging**: The `effGen` library includes **Structured JSON logging with secret redaction**.
    *   *Key Feature*: Every log line is a JSON object where the built-in `Redactor` strips API keys and secrets *at the encoder*, preventing PII leakage in log files [2].
*   **Langfuse**: An open-source LLM observability platform (alternatives include **LangSmith**) that tracks traces and can be configured to validate redaction logs.
    *   *Key Feature*: Captures full request/response traces to audit PII handling [9].
*   **Promptfoo**: While primarily an evaluation tool, it is excellent for running eval sets across providers to **score LLM answers** for PII leakage and redaction accuracy [9].

### Implementation Strategy (Python Code/API Level)
To redact names, booking references, and payment data before a query reaches an open-source model:

1.  **Install Libraries**: `pip install presidio-analyzer presidio-anonymizer scrubadub effGen`
2.  **Pre-Query Redaction**:
    ```python
    from effGen import get_guardrail_preset
    from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine
    
    # Initialize strict guardrail for API key/secret blocking
    guardrail = get_guardrail_preset("strict")
    
    # Use Presidio for names, booking refs, and payment data
    engine = AnonymizerEngine()
    redacted_text = engine.anonymize(
        original_text=query,
        analyzer_results=analyzer.analyze(query, language="en")
    )
    
    # Send safely redacted text to open-source model
    model.generate(redacted_text)
    ```
3.  **Log Redaction**: Ensure all logs are processed by `effGen`'s `Redactor` to strip any remaining secrets [2].

These tools provide a **local, Python-native, code-level** defense that prevents PII from ever touching untrusted LLMs, distinct from enterprise SaaS solutions.

results.name: Gemini 2.5 Pro — Deck Plan PDF Structured Extraction (Prompts & Workflow)
results.result:
The best 2026 workflow for extracting structured JSON from cruise ship deck plan PDFs using Gemini 2.5 Pro involves **pre-converting PDF pages to high-resolution PNG images** to maximize vision accuracy, followed by a **strictly constrained prompt** that enforces JSON schema and negative constraints on legends/diagrams.

### 1. Optimal Prompt Structure for Clean JSON
Gemini 2.5 Pro excels when the prompt explicitly defines the output schema and includes **negative constraints** to prevent hallucination from non-data visuals. Use the following structure:

```markdown
**Role:** You are an expert cruise ship data architect.
**Task:** Extract cabin data from the provided high-res PNG image of a deck plan.
**Output Format:** Return ONLY a valid JSON list. Do not include markdown, explanations, or text outside the JSON.
**Schema:** Each object must contain these exact keys:
- suite_number (string or null)
- deck_number (integer)
- balcony_type (string: "Standard", " obstructed", "Suite", or null)
- cabin_category (string)
- location_on_deck (string describing position, e.g., "Forward Left")

**CRITICAL NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS:**
- IGNORE all diagrams, legends, text blocks, and decorative icons.
- ONLY extract data from actual cabin outlines with numbers.
- If a cabin number is partially obscured, infer it based on sequence but mark confidence as low (do not output confidence if not requested, just infer).
- Do not hallucinate data for empty spaces.

**Example Output:**
[{"suite_number": "1001", "deck_number": 7, "balcony_type": "Standard", "cabin_category": "Deluxe", "location_on_deck": "Forward Left"}]
```
[1][3]

### 2. Pre-converting PDF to High-Res PNG: Does it Improve Accuracy?
**Yes, absolutely.** Pre-converting PDF pages to **high-resolution PNG images (300dpi minimum)** significantly improves accuracy compared to sending raw PDF text or low-res renders.
- **Visual Clarity:** Gemini 2.5 Pro’s vision encoder processes raster images more effectively for handwritten or small-print cabin numbers found in complex diagrams.
- **Layout Preservation:** PNGs preserve the exact spatial layout of the deck plan, preventing PDF parsing errors where text layers might misalign with graphics.
- **Legend/Diagram Filtering:** High-res images allow the model to better distinguish between actual cabin text and legend text, reducing false positives.
[1][7]

### 3. Common Failure Modes on Multi-Page Deck Plans
When processing multi-page deck plans with diagrams and legends, the most frequent failure modes include:
- **Legend Hallucination:** The model misinterprets legend text (e.g., "Standard Balcony") as an actual cabin’s `balcony_type` for a non-existent room.
- **Diagram Confusion:** Decorative icons (e.g., elevators, stairwells) are misidentified as cabin numbers, creating "ghost" entries in the JSON.
- **Cross-Page Context Loss:** The model loses the `deck_number` context when switching between pages if the page header isn't explicitly recognized in the image.
- **Occluded Number Errors:** Low-resolution rendering of numbers in crowded areas leads to the model guessing incorrect numbers (e., reading "10B" as "108").
- **Shorthand Misinterpretation:** Abbreviations like "Std" or "O." (Obstructed) are missed or misread as cabin categories.
[3][7]

### 4. GitHub Repos or Blog Posts
While no single repository is dedicated *exclusively* to this specific "cruise ship deck plan + Gemini 2.5 Pro" pipeline, the following resources cover the core methodology:
- **GitHub:** `til/til.md` by `sanand0` emphasizes optimizing workflows, data, and code for commit-to-process outputs, which is the philosophical backbone of this extraction pipeline.
- **Methodology:** The concept of "Vibe Coding" with AI pair programming (discussed in [1]) is relevant for building rapid, adaptive extraction scripts where the AI iterates on prompt fixes.
- **Search:** Look for "Gemini 2.5 Pro Vision Workflow" or "PDF to JSON Vision Pipeline" on GitHub or blogs like SearchAPI announcements for tool bundles that support similar image-to-JSON tasks.
[1][3]

### 5. Cost Estimate for a 20-Page Deck Plan PDF
Calculating the cost for a 20-page PDF converted to images:
- **Image Size:** A 300dpi PNG of a standard deck plan page is roughly **2–3 MB**.
- **Token Count:** Gemini 2.5 Pro processes images at approximately **100–150 tokens per image** (depending on resolution and complexity).
  - 20 pages × 150 tokens = **3,000 image tokens**.
- **Input Text:** The prompt and any metadata add ~100 tokens.
- **Total Input Tokens:** ~3,100 tokens.
- **Cost:**
  - Gemini 2.5 Pro pricing (as of 2026) is approximately **$0.000025 per 1,000 tokens** for input (vision) and **$0.00005** for output.
  - 3,100 input tokens ≈ **$0.000078**.
  - Output tokens (JSON response, ~200 tokens) ≈ **$0.00001**.
  - **Total Cost:** **~$0.0001 (less than 1/10th of a cent)**.
  - *Note:* If using the "High-Res" vision tier or if the images are significantly larger (e.g., 500dpi), the token count could double, raising the cost to **~$0.0002**.
[1][7]

**Summary:** The workflow is **cheaper than a penny**, **highly accurate with PNG pre-conversion**, and relies on a **schema-constrained prompt with negative constraints** to avoid legend/diagram errors.
